headline: Nine Hours to the East Wall — Bigeye at 2 A.M. and a Marlin We Never Boated
subhead: The run to Atlantis cost us a full tank and a night's sleep, but the temp break paid the diesel bill and then some.
body_markdown:
We left the dock at Montauk at 9 PM Thursday with 340 gallons in the tanks, and I told the mate we'd be lucky to see the rail bend before midnight. That's the math on this run — Atlantis Canyon sits about 100 nautical miles south-southeast of the Point, and at a 24-knot cruise that's four-plus hours just to reach the color change, another hour or two working the edge before you commit to a drift, and then the same four hours home with whatever's in the box. You don't run to the east canyons on a whim. You run because the report, the water temp, and your gut all say the same thing, and this week they did.

We set up on the east wall around 39°49'N, 71°43'W, working a break where the water went from a dirty green-blue into that cobalt you only see when the shelf water's pushed in clean. Trolled a spread of Green Machines and a naked ballyhoo down the middle through the afternoon — one yellowfin in the 40s, lost a wahoo strike that shredded a lure but never came tight, and a white marlin that came up on the long rigger, danced twice, and let go before the mate could get a hand on the leader. That's the canyon for you. It gives you a look and takes it back.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the slot bluefin were holding steady, bigeye showing at the edge, and a marlin raised right where the shelf turns from green-blue to cobalt would confirm what's been building all month. That's exactly what happened out there Thursday night. Once the sun dropped we shut down the trolling gear, drifted the edge, and started chunking butterfish over a slick. Bigeye showed on the sounder around 11 PM, sitting deep — 200, 250 feet — and we picked at them steady through the night on 60-pound fluoro leaders and circle hooks, three fish to the boat before the tide turned against us around 4 AM and the bite went quiet. Not a stacked night, but three bigeye and a keeper yellowfin off one drift is a good return on the fuel burn, and it's the kind of consistency we've been seeing build since mid-July.

The bluefin have been the reliable piece of this puzzle all season — recreational-slot fish scattered along the temperature breaks from Veatch down through Atlantis, mixed in with the yellowfin on the troll during daylight and showing up again on the chunk after dark. Nothing's been a slaughter, but boats working the edges consistently are putting two, three, sometimes four keeper-class bluefin in the box alongside the yellowfin, and that's real money against the diesel bill.

Here's what's changing the calculus for next week: the tide range is narrowing into the coming neap around August 5-6, and that softer current is going to favor the troll over the chunk in the rip-dependent spots. Less current means less bait getting pushed hard against the edges, which means less reason for tuna to hold tight on a slick — they'll be roaming more, and a moving spread covers water a static chunk bait can't. If you're planning a trip this week, I'd lean troll-heavy early, then switch to chunk gear only if you mark fish holding on the sounder rather than just passing through.

Mahi have been a bonus, not a target — a few short bursts of gaffer-class fish under scattered weed lines and the occasional lobster gear float working the flat water between Atlantis and Veatch, taking small chartreuse feathers meant for something bigger. Wahoo remain a low-percentage, high-reward proposition; we've heard of a couple caught on high-speed rigs — Ilanders over cigar minnows run at 12-14 knots — but nobody's targeting them exclusively out here yet. The water hasn't gotten hot enough at depth to concentrate them the way it will later this month.

For boats running out of Block Island or the Rhode Island ports toward Hydrographer and Oceanographer, the extra 20-30 miles of run compared to an Atlantis trip changes the trip planning more than the fishing itself — you're looking at closer to five hours each way at a fuel-conscious cruise, which means committing to an overnight if you want any real time on the grounds. Worth it if the SST breaks are set up right; not worth it if you're just going to poke around. I'd call ahead to whoever's been out there in the last 48 hours before you commit that kind of fuel.

Looking ahead, the stable high pressure that's held all week isn't showing signs of breaking yet, and that's the single biggest reason this bite has stayed consistent instead of going lockjaw. If it holds through the weekend, I'd expect the yellowfin and bluefin pattern to continue on the troll during daylight with the bigeye picking up again after dark on the chunk, especially once the neap current settles in and slows things down enough for a slick to actually hold. Watch for the white marlin to start showing more consistently too — one raised fish is a tease, but the water color and the bait we're seeing say more are coming. If the wind stays out of it, that's where I'd put my next trip.
